title: Are you in the room? A framework for sortition and representation
text:
A thesis submitted for the degree of Bachelor of Commerce (Honours) at Monash University, Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics.

Abstract
Sortition, the random selection of individuals to form deliberative panels, has seen a renaissance in recent years, as institutions realise the value of direct community and stakeholder input in deliberation and policymaking. These panels improve the quality of outcomes, increase public trust and engagement, and create more inclusive processes. Yet little attention has been paid to whether panels preserve a community’s intersectional structure – how demographic traits combine – rather than only its marginal proportions. This thesis uses a simulated sortition pipeline (population, survey sample, and panel selection via the LexiMin algorithm) to test whether quota-constrained selection preserves the joint two-variable association present in a survey sample. Across all simulated conditions, effectively every feasible panel showed a two-variable relationship significantly different from its sample, at a rate far exceeding simple random sampling. These findings motivated Intersection Inspector, a diagnostic Shiny app helping practitioners assess a panel’s representativeness before deliberation begins.
Keywords: sortition; citizens’ assemblies; representativeness; intersectionality; panel selection algorithms

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Background
In a social landscape where the public is growing progressively disillusioned with its representation in politics (Landemore 2026), it is important to consider ways to foster more inclusive decision-making practices. One way of achieving this is using sortition to create panels that are more representative of the population for political discussions and deliberations. Adopted recently by an increasing number of institutions, including the Parisian (“Paris creates a permanent Citizens’ Council” 2021), Irish (Walsh and Elkink 2021), and British Columbian (Ward 2008) governments, sortition as a part of democratic process is gaining traction. As a result, the need for fair and representative methods of building panels is only growing, and progress is being made in improving the structure of selective algorithms. However, there are still many challenges to overcome in order to ensure that these panels consistently achieve the level of representation that they envision. And there remains little procedure on measuring representativeness beyond the “surface” marginal level of demographics.
Sortition is a method of selection that uses random sampling to create panels that should be descriptively representative of a population. It has been used in various contexts, reaching as far back as ancient Athens (where it was how jurors were selected), and now into modern times for citizens’ assemblies. The idea is that randomly selecting individuals from the population can create panels that are more representative and inclusive than those selected through traditional methods, like elections or open-ended surveys. Due to its random nature, sortition also reduces dominance by elites or highly engaged groups, enabling broader participation across social classes (Giuliani 2025), making it more likely that decisions are in the relevant population’s best interest.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
The representation problem
One of the main roadblocks in sortition is ensuring that the selection process is transparent and fair, and that the panels are truly representative of the population in terms of demographics and perspectives. But this raises the questions of what it means to be fair, what it means to be representative, and how these look from a systematic perspective. A fair lottery is not, by itself, proof of a representative outcome – it answers whether everyone had a reasonable chance of being chosen, not whether the people who actually get chosen reflect the community they are meant to stand in for. This thesis is concerned less with whether the process was fair, and more with a plainer question underneath it: who actually ends up on a panel?
As a process, sortition moves through several distinct stages between defining a population and convening a panel (Chapter 2 breaks these down in full), and each one has the potential to introduce bias that compounds by the end – yet there is currently no rigorous evaluation of representation achieved before a deliberative process is run. It is therefore crucial to measure how the level of representativeness (or potential representativeness) flows through each stage, and to understand how different factors may affect it.


Progression of sortition methods
Sortition methods have evolved substantially over time, moving from simple self-selection and proportional sampling toward increasingly systematic algorithmic approaches – LEGACY, MaxiMin, MiniMax, and most recently LexiMin and Goldilocks – each refining how fairly and robustly individual selection probabilities are equalised across a respondent pool (Chapter 2 gives the full history and formal definitions). Of these, LexiMin is the algorithm in practical use today, running inside Panelot (Flanigan et al. 2020), the tool currently used to assemble real sortition panels, and is the algorithm this thesis works with directly.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Thesis scope
All of the aforementioned algorithms only focus on optimising for maximal selection likelihoods as their sole objective functions. This means that in its discovery and construction of feasible panels, the existing LexiMin algorithm may be prone to distortion of intersections and intersectional association trends present within population distributions. This presents a significant risk for the validity of representation achieved by panels output by the algorithm – the extent and reasoning of which will be explored further in the paper.
Additionally, there is limited literature on the visualisations of the outputs of these algorithms. This presents a great opportunity to demystify LexiMin and sortition as a process, improving transparency for practitioners, facilitators, participants, and broader community stakeholders alike. The comparative visualisation methods and tools also allow a general comparison to be made between any selected group and any broader sample it is pulled from, with any algorithm or selection process. This could be useful as a mechanism for quick sanity checks of panel configurations, and as a way for practitioners to evaluate the validity of panels before engaging in deliberation.
To investigate this empirically, this thesis builds a simulated sortition pipeline: synthetic populations with a known, deliberately introduced two-variable association (and a matched population with none), survey samples drawn under both equal-chance and differential response, and panels selected from those samples via LexiMin. Statistical tests then compare each panel’s joint two-variable structure against its own sample, isolating whether a panel’s intersectional composition diverges from the sample it was drawn from beyond what sampling variability alone would produce. The resulting findings motivate a diagnostic Shiny app, Intersection Inspector, that lets practitioners check this directly for their own panels.

Thesis structure
The remainder of this thesis is structured as follows: Chapter 2 provides a literature review of the existing research on sortition and representation, and identifies gaps in the current knowledge. Chapter 3 outlines the simulation-based methodology used to evaluate panel representativeness, including how differential survey non-response is modelled alongside an equal-chance baseline, and the statistical tests used to assess whether a panel’s joint category distribution preserves the association present in the sample it was drawn from. Chapter 4 presents the results of the analysis, showing near-total intersectional association distortion in selected panels, well beyond what a random-sampling benchmark would produce. Chapter 5 introduces “Intersection Inspector”, a tool developed in response to those results to help practitioners assess panel representativeness directly. Chapter 6 concludes by proposing a framework and recommendations for practitioners, discussing the limitations of this thesis, suggesting directions for future research, and reflecting on what genuine representation demands beyond marginal fairness – namely, keeping sight of who the process is meant to represent, and whether it actually does.

text: 2.1 Representation and sortition

title: 2  Literature review
text:
What does it mean to be representative?
Every sortition selection method shares the same basic aim: a panel that is fair and representative of the population. But what does that actually mean?
Fairness means the selection process is transparent, unbiased and inclusive – everyone should have an equal chance of being chosen, regardless of their background or demography. In practice, this comes down to minimising the gap in selection likelihood across the pool, typically achieved by introducing randomness into the process (Flanigan et al. 2021a); without it, selection bias creeps in implicitly.
Representativeness, meanwhile, is about whether the selected panel actually reflects the demographics and perspectives of the population it was drawn from – diverse, inclusive, and populated by people from the range of backgrounds the process set out to capture. This can be checked directly, by comparing a panel’s demographic makeup against the population’s.
Approaching it procedurally, the sortition process can be thought of in four stages:

Defining the population and traits of interest
Sampling from a random subset of the population (through survey or other outreach)
Panel selection (through algorithmic means or other method)
Panel evaluation, confirmation and engagement

Each step is a chance for bias to creep in and representativeness to suffer, which is why it matters to evaluate representativeness (or potential representativeness) at every stage, not just the end.
If the population and the traits of interest are poorly defined, for instance, the selection process may fail to capture the group’s actual diversity, leaving the panel less representative. This is a real challenge in itself: most population descriptions, as discussed above, record demographic characteristics separately rather than capturing how they intersect, which is central to representativeness. Addressing that gap properly would mean wading into broader data collection and storage practices, which is beyond this thesis’s scope – but it is worth keeping in mind that representation goes beyond the margins.
The same applies to survey response: if certain groups are less likely to respond, they end up underrepresented in the pool of potential panelists before a panel is even assembled. If a survey of an area that is 60% women somehow drew no female respondents at all, representativeness would already be violated well before selection begins. Cases like this raise the question of how to account for non-response bias, and whether visualisation can help show the gap between the respondent pool and the population – which is part of what this thesis sets out to do.


Panel selection
Suppose there is a pool of individuals numbered 1 to n, from which a panel of size k is to be chosen. Let K be the set of all feasible panels – any group of k individuals satisfying the required constraints, which generally take the form of quotas.
Quotas specify a desired count, or range of counts, for individuals in a given trait class (e.g. 20-22 males, or 15-17 rural), tied to whichever demographics a project has deemed important to represent. The core goal of sortition, then, is to build a panel that meets those quota constraints equitably, robustly, and in a way that genuinely represents the population it was drawn from.


Existing methods

Non-algorithmic/self-selection
This is the simplest method of panel selection: individuals are simply allowed to self-select, for example by advertising the opportunity and taking sign-ups on a first-come, first-served basis. These methods tend not to produce representative panels, for two reasons. First, they invite self-selection bias – involvement depends on exposure rather than random chance, and the people who put their hand up are more likely to already hold formed opinions, ahead of ever joining the panel. Second, they tend toward lower engagement, since there is no guarantee of reaching a particular level of exposure in the first place.


LEGACY heuristic (Flanigan et al. 2021a; Sortition Foundation 2024)
Already an improvement on non-algorithmic methods, the LEGACY selection heuristic builds a panel by selecting respondents one at a time until it is full. At each step, it calculates a “need” value to find the trait currently furthest from its desired count, then picks a random individual who has that trait. If selecting someone would push a trait past its upper quota, everyone else with that trait is removed from the pool before the next pick. This repeats until the panel is complete, or the process runs out of eligible individuals and restarts. LEGACY satisfies the basic requirement of meeting quotas, but it does not maximise representativeness or fairness: it ignores each individual’s actual selection likelihood (which, in extreme cases, can end up at 0%) and makes no attempt to minimise the maximum deviation from an equal chance of selection. For a time, this was the Sortition Foundation’s own method of panel selection, implemented in their GroupSelect tool, before the algorithmic fairness methods below were developed and adopted.


MaxiMin (Flanigan et al. 2021b) and MiniMax (Baharav and Flanigan 2024)
This shortcoming is addressed by the first two algorithmic sortition methods, MaxiMin and MiniMax, which tackle the problem in opposite ways. MaxiMin generates potential panels and selection probabilities, then sets out to maximise the minimum selection probability across the pool. This reduces the chance of any individual never being picked, improving fairness, but makes the method vulnerable to manipulation – someone who misreports belonging to an under-represented quota group can inflate their own odds. MiniMax instead minimises the maximum selection probability, making selection more robust against manipulation, but at the cost of fairness, since the risk of a 0% selection chance returns.


LexiMin (Flanigan et al. 2021a)
LexiMin – short for Lexicographic MaxiMin – works similarly to MaxiMin, but resolves ties sequentially rather than stopping at the single minimum. It first identifies whoever has the lowest selection chance and maximises that, then moves to the next-lowest, and so on, until every individual’s selection probability has been addressed and made as equal as possible across participants. This gives everyone the highest chance of selection achievable without disadvantaging someone already prioritised – but, like MaxiMin, it inherits a vulnerability to manipulation.


Goldilocks (Baharav and Flanigan 2024)
This brings the discussion to the imminent gold standard: the aptly-named Goldilocks algorithm. Goldilocks simultaneously maximises minimum selection probabilities (for fairness) and minimises maximum selection probabilities (for robustness), aiming for a “best of both worlds” balance between MaxiMin and MiniMax. The motivation is clear: both MaxiMin and LexiMin place no ceiling on how high an individual’s selection probability can climb, so a participant who misreports their trait membership to appear under-represented can disproportionately inflate their own odds. By capping the maximum selection probability, as MiniMax does, Goldilocks limits the payoff from that kind of manipulation while still prioritising the lowest probabilities enough to preserve most of MaxiMin and LexiMin’s fairness guarantees – a selection rule that is simultaneously hard to manipulate and reasonably fair.



Why focus on LexiMin
Goldilocks may be the newer and, in theory, the better algorithm, but this thesis works with LexiMin instead. The reasons are practical. LexiMin is the algorithm actually in use: it runs inside Panelot (Flanigan et al. 2020), the tool practitioners currently use to put real panels together, while no public version of Goldilocks existed at the time of writing. Testing LexiMin means testing the algorithm actually shaping panels today, not one that only exists on paper so far.
It also makes little difference to the specific problem this thesis is looking at. Goldilocks was built to fix manipulation, not to fix how panels handle intersections of traits – and on that front, it works the same way LexiMin does. Both algorithms set selection probabilities purely from marginal quotas, and neither one looks at how traits combine. Capping the highest selection probability, which is all Goldilocks adds on top of LexiMin, has no obvious reason to change how well a panel’s mix of traits reflects its sample. So the gap this chapter identifies below should apply to Goldilocks just as much as it applies to LexiMin. Working with LexiMin here is a matter of what could actually be tested and what practitioners actually use, not a claim that it matters more – the same argument should carry over to Goldilocks once it can be tested directly.

LexiMin approach (Flanigan et al. 2021a)
Rather than committing to a single panel immediately, LexiMin constructs a probability distribution over the full set of feasible panels K, assigning each panel S \in K a non-negative probability p_S that sums to one across the set. An individual’s overall selection chance is then the sum of the probabilities of every panel that includes them. Sorting these chances from smallest to largest, LexiMin proceeds lexicographically: it maximises the smallest probability first, then – holding that value fixed – maximises the second-smallest, and so on until every individual has been addressed.



Formal representation, algorithm and logic
This process can be expressed formally. Let p_S denote the probability assigned to panel S, which must be non-negative and sum to one across every feasible panel in K,

p_S \ge 0, \qquad \sum_{S \in K} p_S = 1.
\tag{2.1}
The resulting selection probability for an individual i is the sum of the probabilities of every feasible panel containing them, giving the full vector of individual selection probabilities across the population,

\pi_i(p) = \sum_{S \in K,\ i \in S} p_S, \qquad \pi(p) = (\pi_1(p), \pi_2(p), \ldots, \pi_n(p)).
\tag{2.2}
Sorted from smallest to largest, \pi_{(1)}(p) \le \pi_{(2)}(p) \le \ldots \le \pi_{(n)}(p), LexiMin chooses the distribution p that maximises this vector in lexicographic order – the smallest entry first, then the second-smallest subject to the first remaining maximised, and so on down the vector.
In practice, this runs as a sequence of steps: every feasible panel in K is listed alongside every possible probability distribution over those panels, and each candidate distribution’s resulting selection probabilities are computed and sorted as above. Only the distribution (or distributions) that maximise the smallest probability \pi_{(1)}(p) are retained; if several remain tied, this narrows further to those that also maximise the second-smallest, and so on, resolving ties one probability at a time until a single distribution remains, from which a final panel is then selected.
At its core, then, LexiMin is purely a fairness rule: it prioritises whoever has the lowest chance of selection, improves their odds first, then works through the next-lowest probabilities until no further improvement is possible without disadvantaging someone already prioritised – leaving selection probabilities as equal as possible across the population, within the panel’s quota constraints.

title: 2  Literature review
text:
2.2 Visualisation methods
Current sortition practice communicates a sample or panel’s composition almost exclusively through pie charts, or bar charts showing the same information in a different shape – one chart per demographic category, each showing that variable’s marginal breakdown in isolation. Both are easy to produce and easy for a non-specialist audience to read at a glance, which likely explains their popularity with practitioners reporting on panel composition. But neither can encode more than a single categorical variable at a time: there is no visual channel left over to show how two variables relate to one another. For example, a practitioner working only from pie or bar charts can confirm that a panel’s age breakdown looks right, and separately that its tenure breakdown looks right, but has no way of seeing whether the right combinations of age and tenure made it onto the panel. Faceting a bar chart by a second variable does not fix this: each facet’s bars are rescaled relative to that facet alone, rather than the whole population, so an association between the two variables – which can only be seen when proportions stay relative to the full population – is exactly what gets obscured by splitting the chart apart in the first place.
Mosaic plots are a longstanding answer to exactly this limitation. A mosaic plot divides a rectangle into tiles whose widths and heights are proportional to the categories of two (or more) variables, so that each tile’s area represents the joint frequency of that specific combination, rather than either variable’s marginal frequency alone (Hofmann 2003). Graphical methods for categorical data are comparatively underdeveloped next to those available for numeric data, and mosaic plots have been established in the statistical graphics literature as one of the more effective options for visualising relationships between multiple categorical variables at once. Because tile area scales with both variables simultaneously, a departure from proportional tiling signals that the two variables are not independent, in a way no pie chart or ordinary bar chart can show. The current R package for building mosaic plots within the ggplot2 grammar of graphics is ggmosaic2 (Friendly et al. 2026), an actively maintained extension of the original ggmosaic implementation (Jeppson et al. 2026).

title: 2  Literature review
text:
2.3 Discussion and new investigation
This approach is effective at making selection probabilities as equal as possible, which helps make sortition fairer by reducing situations where specific individuals are disadvantaged. It does not, however, provide any way to impose joint trait requirements on subsets of the population – something that may be necessary for accurate representation of community groups. That gap reflects a broader pattern across this literature: algorithmic effort has gone almost entirely into optimising the fairness and robustness of the selection mechanism, rather than validating the outcome that mechanism produces. A panel satisfying every fairness and robustness guarantee an algorithm offers is not thereby guaranteed to represent the population it was drawn from well – these are related but distinct properties, and the literature so far has focused heavily on the former at the expense of the latter, undermining representativeness as a goal given the motivation for sortitioned panels in the first place: filling a room with individuals who accurately and descriptively reflect a community’s population diversity and characteristics.
One specific way this gap shows up: no algorithmic technique surveyed here stratifies for combinations of demographic traits in its decision-making – each instead affects individual selection chances purely through quotas set on each trait at the margin. This is a real limitation, since it means the selection process may fail to capture the group’s actual diversity, leaving a less representative panel. In some situations – side-panels built for specific subgroups, or communities with known intersectional minorities of interest – ensuring specific intersectional combinations are included may be necessary for genuine representation. This gap is generally patched in practice by bringing in “specialist speakers” during deliberation (Redman and Carson n.d.), but that is a different kind of inclusion than being part of the panel and its decision-making directly.
Notably, this gap is rarely argued for directly; it is largely left unaddressed. The implicit assumption running through this literature appears to be that satisfying marginal quotas is enough – that selecting individuals to hit the right counts for each trait independently will, through the randomness built into the selection mechanism, naturally produce a panel whose combinations of traits are also reasonably representative, without this needing to be checked or enforced directly. None of the algorithmic methods reviewed above test whether this actually holds, and the literature more broadly does not appear to examine it either.
This thesis treats that assumption as an open empirical question rather than a safe default. The simulations that follow test how much intersectional inclusion happens naturally under current methods, and establish a way to measure how much intersectionality and association survives the selection process.

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.1 Research aims
This thesis set out to assess whether current algorithmic methods achieve representative panels, diagnose whether a sample’s association trends survive the sortition process, demystify sortition selection to improve its transparency, and provide a framework for more informed, standardised practitioner decisions.
Underlying these aims is a more basic question: what does it mean for a panel to be “good” at representation, and are current methods actually achieving it? That breaks down further. Are algorithms like LexiMin performing as well as they could? How well do intersectional associations and trends survive selection, and therefore how representative is panel composition? And how much can differing survey response rates and other sampling-level issues bias representativeness, beyond whatever the algorithm itself contributes?

title: 3  Methodology
text:
3.2 Research design

Simulation design
To test these questions, two populations of simple intersectional complexity (two variables) with varying associations (independent and associated) were simulated. The findings should generalise to cases with more categories, and are expected to be more severe there, since the intersectional matrix only grows in dimension while panel size stays fixed. The categories used – age (18-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65+) and tenure status (rent, own, other) – were chosen to mirror demographic variables commonly used for sortition in practice. Combining these two variables produced the four simulated sample/respondent datasets used for panel selection.


Population, slice, sample and panel: procedure and definitions
Every simulated dataset in this thesis moves through the same four stages, with terms kept deliberately consistent throughout to avoid ambiguity – “sample” in particular is used loosely, and inconsistently, across much of the sortition literature.

Population: the full simulated universe of individuals (n_{\text{total}} = 100{,}000), generated from a specified joint probability array over the category variables. This represents the entire community eligible for selection, with marginal and joint (intersectional) distributions known exactly, since they were specified directly in the data-generating process.
Slice: a simple random sample, without replacement, of 10% of the population, drawn before any response behaviour is simulated – representing the group actually invited to take part (e.g. mailed a survey), sometimes called the invited pool elsewhere. Because it is drawn uniformly at random, the slice’s composition deviates from the population’s only through ordinary sampling variability, not systematic bias.
Sample: the subset of the slice who actually respond, determined by an independent Bernoulli trial for each invited individual under one of the response-rate cases described below. This is the realised pool available for panel selection – also called the respondent pool or survey sample elsewhere – and the benchmark every panel’s representativeness is compared against, since it, not the full population, is what any practical algorithm actually draws from.
Panel: a fixed-size subset of k members drawn from the sample by a selection algorithm (LexiMin, via Panelot, in current practice) subject to quota constraints on each category level’s permitted count – the final body that would convene to deliberate, and the unit whose representativeness this thesis is ultimately concerned with.









Figure 3.1: The four stages of the simulation pipeline: population, slice, sample and panel.





Figure 3.1 summarises this pipeline. Each stage can introduce its own departure from the population’s true composition: the slice through ordinary sampling variability, the sample through differential response rates, and the panel through the selection algorithm’s own quota mechanism (Section 3.2.5). Distinguishing these stages explicitly makes it possible to attribute any observed distortion in a final panel to a specific stage of the pipeline, rather than to sortition “in general”.


Population construction: age and tenure
To illustrate the general procedure concretely at a minimal scale, this thesis builds a simple two-variable example using only age and tenure. Age is denoted A, taking one of L_A = 5 ordered levels a \in \{1, \dots, 5\} (18-34 through 65+), and tenure is denoted T, taking one of L_T = 3 levels t \in \{1, \dots, 3\} (Rent, Own, Other). Marginal probability vectors were defined for each variable,

\mathbf{p}_A = \left(p_{A_1}, \dots, p_{A_5}\right), \qquad \mathbf{p}_T = \left(p_{T_1}, p_{T_2}, p_{T_3}\right), \qquad \sum_{a=1}^{5} p_{A_a} = 1, \qquad \sum_{t=1}^{3} p_{T_t} = 1,
\tag{3.1}
with \mathbf p_A = (0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.25, 0.15), a mild skew toward the upper-middle age brackets, and \mathbf p_T = (0.30, 0.50, 0.20), a moderate skew toward home ownership. Both the independent and associated populations below use these same marginal targets, so any difference between them is attributable solely to the association introduced, not to a difference in either variable’s marginal distribution.
An independent population (sim_data2) was generated by taking the outer product of these two marginals to form a joint probability array,

P^{(0)}(a, t) \;=\; p_{A_a} \, p_{T_t}, \qquad \mathbf{P}^{(0)} \;=\; \mathbf{p}_A \mathbf{p}_T^\top \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{5 \times 3},
\tag{3.2}
a 5 \times 3 matrix whose row sums equal \mathbf p_A and column sums equal \mathbf p_T by construction, so that A \perp T. This array was flattened into a probability vector and cell counts were drawn from a single multinomial trial before being expanded into individual-level records, as described in full below.
A second, associated population (sim_data2_cov) uses the same marginal targets but deliberately introduces a negative association between age and renting, via an ordinal score for age,

s(a) = \frac{a - 1}{5 - 1} \in [0, 1],
\tag{3.3}
running from 0 for the youngest bracket to 1 for the oldest, which was used to seed the independent array \mathbf P^{(0)} with an exponential adjustment factor targeting only the “Rent” level of tenure,

\tilde{P}(a, t) \;=\; P^{(0)}(a, t) \cdot \exp\!\Big(-\alpha \, s(a) \cdot \mathbb{1}[t = \text{Rent}]\Big), \qquad \alpha = 1.2,
\tag{3.4}
scaling down the probability of renting by a factor of e^{-\alpha s(a)} that grows with age, while leaving owning and other tenure unchanged. Because this adjustment only touches the “Rent” column, the row and column sums of \tilde{\mathbf P} no longer equal \mathbf p_A and \mathbf p_T, so the array was rescaled through iterative proportional fitting (raking) to restore the age and tenure marginals exactly to their specified targets. Repeating this two-pass rescaling for R = 100 iterations (well past convergence for a 5 \times 3 table; full update rule in Appendix A) yields a raked array P^\star satisfying \sum_{t} P^\star(a, t) = p_{A_a} for all a and \sum_{a} P^\star(a, t) = p_{T_t} for all t, to numerical tolerance, while retaining the negative age-renting association introduced by the exponential seeding step – raking restores the specified marginals while preserving the association the adjustment introduced.
Both populations were sampled the same way, differing only in which array was used. The relevant array (\mathbf P^{(0)} for the independent case, or the raked P^\star for the associated case) was flattened into a probability vector \mathbf p^\star \in \mathbb R^{15} (age varying fastest), and cell counts were drawn from a single multinomial trial,

(n_1, \dots, n_{15}) \sim \text{Multinomial}\!\left(n_{\text{total}}, \, \mathbf p^\star\right), \qquad n_{\text{total}} = 100{,}000,
\tag{3.5}
with each cell j, corresponding to one (a, t) combination, expanded into n_j individual-level records sharing that age and tenure. Comparing the two resulting populations demonstrates the core logic of the simulation framework in its simplest form: a chi-squared test of association between age and tenure is non-significant in the independent population but highly significant in the associated population, with the conditional probability of renting falling steadily from around 44% among 18-34 year olds to around 18% among those aged 65 and over, even though both populations share identical marginal distributions for age and tenure individually. This confirms the seeding-and-raking procedure successfully introduces a targeted association without disturbing the overall marginal proportions, and sets up a direct test of whether the selection algorithm preserves intersection structure beyond the purely marginal level.


Slice and sample construction: response simulation
As is standard practice, a random slice of the population (10%) is taken to serve as the survey sample, from which responses are drawn. Concretely, from a population of n_{\text{total}} individuals, a survey sample \mathcal{S} of size n_{\mathcal S} = \lfloor 0.10 \, n_{\text{total}} \rceil (so n_{\mathcal S} = 10{,}000 for the two-variable example, drawn uniformly at random without replacement) is taken as the invited pool, before any response behaviour is simulated. Whether each invited individual i \in \mathcal S actually responds is then modelled by a binary response variable R, with R_i = 1 if individual i responds and R_i = 0 otherwise, drawn as an independent Bernoulli trial,

R_i \;\overset{\text{ind.}}{\sim}\; \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_i),
\tag{3.6}
where the response probability \pi_i is assigned according to one of two cases: an independent case, and an age-covaried case mirroring the age-renting association introduced at the population level above.
In the independent case, every invited individual is equally likely to respond regardless of their trait profile,

\pi_i = \pi_0, \qquad \pi_0 = 0.30,
\tag{3.7}
a baseline against which the effects of differential response can be compared; a chi-squared test confirms no significant association between A and R here, as expected. In the age-covaried case, response likelihood increases with age, reusing the same ordinal score s(a) defined above,

\pi_i = \pi_1 \exp\!\big(\alpha_R \, s(a_i)\big), \qquad \pi_1 = 0.20, \quad \alpha_R = 1.0,
\tag{3.8}
so that the response rate rises from around 20% among the youngest bracket to over 50% among the oldest, and the association between A and R is now highly significant.
Applying both response cases to both populations produces four respondent-pool files – sim_data2_ind_eq.csv, sim_data2_ind_ass.csv, sim_data2_cov_eq.csv and sim_data2_cov_ass.csv – each containing only the individuals who actually responded under that population/response-case combination, with their age and tenure. These names follow the same <ind|cov>_<eq|ass> convention used for the lottery files below, so a file name alone identifies both the population and response case it came from. Each respondent pool is, in the terminology above, a sample: the realised pool a panel can actually be drawn from, and the input to the panel-selection step described next.


Panel generation and evaluation

Panel generation and representation
With the four respondent-pool files constructed above, the final stage of the pipeline draws an actual panel from each respondent pool. This was done using Panelot, a sortition tool that selects panels of a fixed size k (here k = 50) subject to quota constraints on each variable’s margin independently – a minimum and maximum permitted count for every age bracket and tenure category, based on the population’s marginal distributions and specified in a categories.csv file. For brackets whose exact proportional target at k = 50 was non-integer – 18-34, 45-54, 55-64 and 65+, each targeting 7.5 or 12.5 members – the quota range was set to the floor and ceiling of that target (e.g. 7-8 for a 7.5 target). The remaining categories – 35-44 and all three tenure levels – land on exact integer targets and so carry a fixed quota with no slack. Rather than a single fixed panel, Panelot’s output, lottery.csv, enumerates every feasible panel its selection algorithm discovered, together with the exact probability q_j panel j would be returned were the lottery run, so \sum_j q_j = 1 across the J discovered panels. Each row lists the pool identifiers of the k = 50 selected respondents.
A deliberate feature of this quota structure is that it constrains the age and tenure margins of a panel separately, with no quota placed on their joint (intersectional) distribution. Two panels can therefore satisfy identical quotas – the same count of 18-34 year olds, the same count of renters – while differing substantially in which individuals combine which age with which tenure. This asymmetry between marginal and joint representativeness motivates the association-level evaluation developed below.
Four lottery files were generated in this way, covering every combination of the two populations (independent and associated) and the two response-rate cases (equal-chance and age-associated) introduced previously: lottery_ind_eq.csv, lottery_ind_ass.csv, lottery_cov_eq.csv and lottery_cov_ass.csv. Each panel’s members are identified only by pool identifier in lottery.csv, so their age and tenure values were recovered by joining back onto the respondent-pool CSV originally supplied to Panelot (e.g. sim_data2_cov_eq.csv). This respondent pool – the people who were invited to respond and actually did so – is referred to throughout as the survey sample, and serves as the benchmark against which every panel’s composition is compared.


Panel-versus-sample homogeneity test
For each discovered panel j, a 5 \times 3 contingency table of age against tenure was constructed from its k = 50 members, and a chi-squared test of independence applied to assess whether age and tenure appear related within that panel alone. With only 50 observations spread across 15 cells, several expected cell counts fall below the conventional rule-of-thumb minimum of five, so a Monte Carlo approximation to the null distribution (simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000 resamples) replaced the standard asymptotic chi-squared reference distribution.
This within-panel test alone cannot establish whether a panel’s association differs from the survey sample’s – a panel could show a significant association purely because the sample itself does. To test this directly, each panel j was compared against the remainder of the survey sample via a three-way log-linear model. Writing G for a binary group indicator (panel member vs. not), a Poisson model was fitted to the cell counts of the 5 \times 3 \times 2 Age \times Tenure \times G table, first without the three-way interaction,

\log \mathbb{E}[\text{Freq}] = \beta_0 + \beta_A^{(a)} + \beta_T^{(t)} + \beta_G^{(g)} + \beta_{AT}^{(a,t)} + \beta_{AG}^{(a,g)} + \beta_{TG}^{(t,g)},
\tag{3.9}
and then with it,

\log \mathbb{E}[\text{Freq}] = \beta_0 + \beta_A^{(a)} + \beta_T^{(t)} + \beta_G^{(g)} + \beta_{AT}^{(a,t)} + \beta_{AG}^{(a,g)} + \beta_{TG}^{(t,g)} + \beta_{ATG}^{(a,t,g)}.
\tag{3.10}
A likelihood-ratio test between these two nested models isolates the three-way interaction term \beta_{ATG}, with the test statistic G^2 = 2(\ell_{\text{full}} - \ell_{\text{reduced}}) referred to a \chi^2_8 distribution – 8 degrees of freedom corresponding to the (5-1)(3-1)(2-1) free parameters contributed by \beta_{ATG}^{(a,t,g)} across the 5 \times 3 \times 2 table. Rather than testing whether the fitted \hat\beta_{ATG} is itself close to zero, the test asks whether allowing the age-tenure association to differ between panel and non-panel members improves the model’s fit by more than chance alone would produce. A significant result indicates that the age-tenure association differs between panel members and the rest of the sample, i.e. that panel j’s intersectional composition is not merely a smaller, noisier version of the sample’s, but systematically different from it.
Because every panel discovered for a given lottery file is tested this way – several thousand panels per file – the homogeneity test was repeated many times over. Results are reported at an uncorrected threshold of \alpha = 0.05 throughout.
A panel of only 50 members is itself a small sample, so some disagreement with the full survey sample’s association is expected from sampling variability alone, independent of anything specific to Panelot’s mechanism. To separate a genuine quota-constrained-selection effect from this baseline noise, the same homogeneity test was applied to 500 simple random samples of size 50, drawn without quota constraints from the same survey sample. If panels were no more divergent from the sample than equivalently sized random draws, the proportion flagged as significantly different should resemble the proportion of random samples flagged – approximately \alpha under the null.
Alongside each test, Cramer’s V,

V = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2 / n}{\min(r - 1, \, c - 1)}},
\tag{3.11}
was computed from the within-panel contingency table, with r = 5 age brackets as rows and c = 3 tenure categories as columns (an arbitrary orientation choice, since \min(r-1, c-1) is unaffected by swapping which variable is assigned to rows versus columns), to express the strength, rather than merely the statistical significance, of the association detected within each panel.



Validating the simulation: numerical summary
Alongside the mosaic plots used throughout this thesis to compare the age x tenure population, slice and respondent sample visually (Chapter 2; visualisation methods are discussed further below), each simulated dataset is also checked numerically, to confirm the data-generating process behaved as intended before any downstream panel evaluation. Two quantities recur throughout this checking, the same chi-squared logic underlying the panel-level homogeneity test described above (Section 3.2.5):

A chi-squared test of independence, applied to the 5 \times 3 age-by-tenure contingency table, confirms whether the intended association (or lack of it) was actually realised in a given dataset. A non-significant result (p > 0.05) for the independent population (sim_data2), alongside a significant result for the associated population (sim_data2_cov), is the expected pattern – a sanity check on the simulation code, not a substantive finding in its own right.
Marginal proportion tables (prop.table() applied to the age and tenure frequency tables) confirm that each variable’s marginal distribution matches its specified target (\mathbf p_A or \mathbf p_T) to within sampling error, at both the population and sample level. This matters particularly for the associated population, where raking is specifically designed to restore exact marginal targets despite the association-inducing adjustment applied beforehand.



Visualisation methods
The choice of visualisation follows from the nature of the data. The variables of interest – age brackets, tenure status, and other demographic categories used for sortition – are categorical rather than continuous, and the central question is how they intersect, not how any one is distributed alone. Scatterplots and histograms are built for continuous data; a bar or pie chart shows one categorical variable’s marginal distribution but not how two or more co-occur (Section 4.1); and a bar chart grouped by a second variable becomes hard to read once cell counts are uneven – precisely this thesis’s situation – because bar heights are not comparable the way proportional tile areas are. The mosaic plot, by contrast, represents both marginal and joint distributions within a single figure (Chapter 2), which is why it is the primary visualisation tool used throughout this thesis: it shows not just whether individual categories are represented in the right proportions, but whether particular combinations are over- or under-represented relative to population demographics. Mosaic plots were constructed using the ggmosaic2 package (Friendly et al. 2026), built within the ggplot2 grammar of graphics.
To make later plots easy to interpret, the simplest form of a mosaic plot is shown in Figure 3.2 below.








Figure 3.2: A simple mosaic plot of favourite fruit (x-axis) against favourite ice cream flavour (fill), illustrating the mosaic plot convention used throughout this thesis. The two bars are split in opposite directions, illustrating a clear association between the variables.





This example uses two variables, favourite fruit and favourite ice cream, with 25 individuals per fruit (50 total) and ice cream deliberately associated with fruit – 80% of Apple-lovers prefer Vanilla, 80% of Orange-lovers prefer Strawberry. Bar width reflects each category’s marginal share (equal here); fill height reflects the conditional proportion of ice cream given fruit. The association appears in the fill split, which reverses almost entirely between bars, so fruit preference is highly informative about ice cream preference. Had the variables been independent, both bars would show close to a 50/50 split regardless of bar width: a difference in fill proportions, not bar width, is what signals an association, as with the independent and associated age-tenure populations introduced above.
This convention – x-axis width proportional to marginal share, fill height proportional to conditional proportion – is used throughout for the population, slice and sample comparisons, with age brackets on the x-axis and tenure as fill.


Method limitations and caveats
The response rates used for the age x tenure pipeline – 30% baseline, rising above 50% in the age-covaried case – are considerably higher than typical real-world sortition response rates, often below 10%. This was deliberate: lower rates, applied to a 10,000-person slice, would leave too few respondents in some of the 15 age-by-tenure cells to reliably assess quota satisfaction or intersectional preservation at k = 50, leaving the algorithm data-starved regardless of its own effectiveness. Elevating the response rate instead isolates the algorithm’s own behaviour as the object of study, so any representativeness issues identified here are a conservative, best-case estimate: realistic response rates would leave even less data to work with, and more room for poorly representative panels.
Every association introduced in the pipeline – age-renting at the population level (\alpha = 1.2) and age-response at the sampling level (\alpha_R = 1.0) – used a single exponential strength parameter, fixed at a moderate-to-strong value chosen to be clearly visible in a mosaic plot and reliably detectable by a chi-squared test. These values are not derived from any real-world dataset, and performance is unlikely to degrade uniformly with association strength: a weaker but evenly spread association might survive a process that fails here, while an association resting on fewer individuals could be disrupted more easily even if comparably strong. Because this simulation uses fixed strengths rather than a systematic sweep, the panel-level results in Section 4.3 should be read as showing that failures of this kind are possible and can be severe at the strength simulated, not as a generalisable estimate of their magnitude in practice.
A further question is what a panel’s divergence from its sample actually shows, not just how large it is. Panelot’s quotas come from each category’s population marginal distribution, not the marginals actually seen in the sample a panel is drawn from (Section 3.2.5), so a panel satisfying population-based quotas could in principle diverge from its sample on exactly those margins, simply because the sample has drifted from the population through sampling variability or differential non-response. This is not a concern for the test behind this thesis’s headline results, however: the panel-versus-sample test underlying Table 4.2’s “significantly different” flag (Section 3.2.5) uses a three-way age-by-tenure-by-group interaction term whose null model already lets age and tenure vary freely by group, so only a genuine difference in the age-tenure association – not in either group’s marginals – can trigger it. Since Panelot’s quotas are marginal-only, population-based correction cannot register as a false divergence here. The exception is the standalone Cramer’s V figures reported alongside this test (e.g. in Table 4.2 and Table 4.3), which are computed per table rather than as a group comparison and so remain sensitive to marginal drift.
This also explains why the survey sample, not the population, is used as the benchmark throughout this thesis: a practitioner running a real sortition process has no access to the population’s joint age-tenure distribution to check a panel against – intersectional population data is rarely published, a gap this thesis works around rather than closes (Chapter 2) – and quotas are set from population marginals for the same reason. The survey sample is therefore the best source of joint information available, making the panel-versus-sample comparison used throughout Section 3.2.5 and Section 4.3 the most direct representativeness test practically achievable.

4.1 The problem with current visualisations
Before turning to this thesis’s main results, it is worth demonstrating directly why mosaic plots – rather than the pie charts (or equivalent bar charts) that commonly accompany a sample or panel’s reported composition in current sortition practice – are used throughout this chapter, rather than simply asserting it (Chapter 3).
Figure 4.1: Pie charts displaying age (left column) and tenure (right column) marginal proportions for the independent population (top) and associated population (bottom). The age categories range from 15%-25% and roughly half of the population owns their home. Notably, these marginal distributions are exactly the same, which hides any association.
Figure 4.1 uses this thesis’s own independent and associated populations (sim_data2, sim_data2_cov) to make the point concrete: the raking procedure used to build the associated population restores the independent population’s marginals while retaining the age-renting association introduced beforehand (Chapter 3), so the largest gap between the two populations’ marginal proportions, across any single age bracket or tenure category, is only 0.02 percentage points – attributable to sampling noise alone.
Yet the two populations are not the same: the associated population carries a genuine, and statistically detectable (Table 4.1), negative association between age and renting, while the independent population has none at all. A pie chart – or a bar chart, which encodes exactly the same single-variable information in a different shape – has no visual channel available to show this: it can only display one categorical variable’s marginal distribution at a time, so two variables each need their own, entirely separate chart, and nothing in either chart can reveal how the two co-occur. A practitioner shown only the pie charts in Figure 4.1 would have no way of telling the independent and associated populations apart, despite one holding a materially different – and, as Section 4.3 goes on to show, selection-relevant – relationship between age and tenure than the other. The mosaic plots used throughout the remainder of this chapter (Chapter 3) exist specifically to close this gap, representing both variables’ marginal distributions and their joint, intersectional distribution within a single figure.

Table 4.2 summarises the results across all four lottery files. In the associated population, the survey sample itself retains a clearly detectable age-tenure association (Cramer’s V around 0.13), consistent with the negative age-renting relationship built into the population design. In the independent population, by contrast, the sample-level association is negligible and statistically indistinguishable from zero (both p > 0.5), exactly as expected given no association was introduced between age and tenure at the population level.
Despite this contrast in the underlying samples, the proportion of panels flagged as holding a significantly different association from their sample is strikingly similar – and strikingly high – across all four files: between 99.8% and 100%. In other words, essentially every panel Panelot could possibly return, under either population structure and either response-rate case, exhibits an age-tenure relationship detectably different from the sample it was drawn from – including in the independent population, where there is no true association for a panel to even distort.
Splitting this range apart by file shows little further structure: the two equal-chance lotteries (lottery_cov_eq.csv, lottery_ind_eq.csv) each flag 100% of their feasible panels, while the two age-associated lotteries fall only fractionally short, at 99.93% and 99.77% respectively – despite these two files containing roughly twice as many feasible panels (2981 and 3483, against 1867 and 1516), and therefore more opportunities for an occasional panel to be drawn that does not diverge from its sample. Neither population structure nor response case moves the result in a way that a difference of a few feasible panels out of several thousand cannot already explain – the distortion identified here looks like a property of the quota mechanism itself, not of any particular population or response structure it happens to be applied to.
This saturation pattern also speaks to a design concern about the panel-versus-sample test raised in Section 3.2.5: because Panelot’s quota constraints are set from each category’s population marginal distribution rather than the survey sample’s own marginals, a panel could in principle diverge from its sample simply because the sample’s composition has drifted from the population’s, rather than because of anything specific to the selection mechanism. Under equal-chance response, however, the survey sample’s age marginal already matches the population’s closely (Figure 4.2, Figure 4.3), leaving barely any population-versus-sample gap for population-based quotas to correct – yet the equal-chance files above are flagged as different at least as often as the age-associated ones, where the sample’s marginal has genuinely drifted from the population’s (Figure 4.4, Figure 4.5). If population correction were driving the divergence, equal-chance panels should have been flagged less often, not equally or more. Together with the test’s own design – which already allows panel and sample to differ freely on each marginal without that alone counting as significant (Section 3.2.5) – this confirms that the near-total divergence documented here reflects the quota mechanism leaving the joint age-tenure distribution unconstrained, rather than any population-versus-sample drift.

Although the panel satisfies the same marginal age and tenure quotas as the sample, its age-tenure combinations are considerably more blocky and uneven – several age brackets end up filled by entirely one tenure category, exaggerating the sample’s already-present age-renting association.





Figure 4.6 makes explicit what the aggregate figures above describe in summary: the smooth, gradually strengthening sample-level relationship between age and renting gives way to a considerably more extreme, blocky panel-level pattern, despite the panel satisfying the same marginal quotas as the sample it was ostensibly drawn to represent.
