Even though age and tenure carry no association in the sample – its fill proportions sit close to flat across every age bracket – the panel still ends up blocky and uneven, with most age brackets dominated by a single tenure category, showing the distortion is an artefact of selection itself rather than an exaggeration of a real trend.





Figure 4.7 shows the same comparison for the independent population. The panel is, if anything, more extreme than the associated-population example: the within-panel test gives a Cramer’s V of 0.9, versus 0.03 for the sample it was drawn from. Because this panel’s distorted joint structure cannot be attributed to a genuine association it is “exaggerating” – there is none to exaggerate in the independent population – it most directly demonstrates that the within-panel association test is picking up an artefact of the selection mechanism, not a real signal faithfully (if imperfectly) carried through from the sample.


Summary
Across all four simulated conditions, satisfying Panelot’s marginal quotas on age and tenure did not translate into a panel whose joint age-tenure structure resembled its survey sample’s: essentially every feasible panel was flagged as significantly different from the sample, at a rate far beyond what panel size alone could explain, and this held regardless of whether the underlying population carried a genuine age-tenure association or response was skewed by age. Marginal quota satisfaction – the only form of representativeness that a current sortition tool like Panelot reports to a practitioner – is therefore not a reliable proxy for intersectional representativeness in this simulation, and the gap between the two looks like a structural consequence of leaving the joint distribution unconstrained, rather than an artefact of this thesis’s particular panel size or association strengths. This divergence is not attributable to panels merely correcting toward population marginals where the sample itself has drifted – a possibility already ruled out above, both by the panel-versus-sample test’s design and by the data (Section 4.3; Chapter 3). Chapter 5 introduces Intersection Inspector, a tool built directly in response to this marginal-versus-intersectional gap, which displays a panel’s intersectional association alongside its marginal quota satisfaction so that this kind of distortion is visible to a practitioner before a panel convenes, rather than only to a reader of this thesis after the fact.

title: 5  Introducing Intersection Inspector
text:
5.1 Context: prior steps in the sortition pipeline
Having flagged the issues with current sortition methods and process, the second gap this thesis set out to address was the absence of a tool for practitioners to assess the viability and intersectionality of panels before deliberation begins. To that end, a Shiny app was developed. Even in current practice, the LexiMin lottery and panel selection process takes two steps: uploading categories, trait quotas and a respondent pool with the desired panel size, then taking the resulting lottery to a separate interactive page for random number generation to select a specific panel. This thesis’s app replaces that second step, with added functionality that smooths a practitioner’s workflow and gives them more confidence in a panel’s representativeness at a controllably granular level of intersectionality – enabling more informed decisions about quota adjustments and representative validity, and reducing the likelihood of unexpectedly poor intersectional spread when panels convene.
Intersection Inspector is not intended to replace the sortition process as a whole, only its final step. By the time a practitioner opens the app, they are assumed to have already carried out the preceding stages of a sortition: recruiting and surveying a respondent pool, specifying the category variables and trait quotas the panel should satisfy (e.g. minimum and maximum counts per age bracket, per tenure category), and running a selection algorithm over that pool to discover every panel of the desired size that satisfies those quotas. In current practice this selection step is performed by LexiMin, through the Panelot app hosted at Panelot.org, which outputs a lottery file enumerating each feasible panel together with its probability of being returned.
The app takes this lottery file and the underlying respondent pool as given, and does not re-run or second-guess the algorithm that produced them. Its usefulness is therefore not tied to LexiMin specifically: any sortition algorithm or process producing an equivalent output – a set of feasible panels (or a single panel) drawn from a known respondent pool, satisfying some quota specification – could be inspected through the app the same way. The quota-based selection step and the intersectional evaluation step addressed here are conceptually separate, and the latter is agnostic to which algorithm performed the former.

title: 5  Introducing Intersection Inspector
text:
5.2 Intended workflow
The app page consists of three parts: 1. a sidebar comprised of interactable buttons, toggles and sliders, 2. a window that displays mosaic plots comparing the 2-way intersections and associations present between the sample and any selected panel for any two selected category variables, and 3. a window that displays the relative proportions of every trait present in the sample and any selected panel, across all categories present within the sample’s dataset. Figure 5.1 shows all three parts together, using the associated population’s equal-chance lottery (lottery_cov_eq.csv) – the same example used for Figure 4.6 in Chapter 4 – as the uploaded sample and lottery file. To make use of this, a practitioner is expected to follow the below procedure.






Figure 5.1: Intersection Inspector’s main view: the sidebar (left) for file upload, variable selection and panel navigation; the “Survey Sample vs. Panel” mosaic comparison (top right); and the “Marginal trait distributions” bar chart (bottom right). Shown here with the same associated-population, equal-chance example (lottery_cov_eq.csv) used in Figure 4.6.




Uploading files
Intersection Inspector takes two files as input: the sample file the lottery was drawn from (the respondent pool that was invited and agreed to participate) and a lottery file (Panelot’s lottery.csv, enumerating every panel the sortition algorithm found feasible, each with its member IDs and return probability). From these two files alone, the app reconstructs every selected panel’s composition on each category present in the sample and makes its intersectional structure directly inspectable, without the practitioner writing any code or leaving the browser.


Required file structure
Because the app is designed to work with any sortition process producing an equivalent output, not just this thesis’s own simulation (Chapter 5), it does not hard-code column names or category domains. Instead, it expects each uploaded file to follow a general structure – the same structure Panelot itself produces, and the one this thesis’s own simulated data (Chapter 3) is written out in.
The sample file (the respondent pool, or survey sample, a lottery was drawn from) should hold one row per respondent, with:

an optional ID column, detected case-insensitively by header name (pool_member_identifier, id, member_id, respondent_id, or identifier); if none of these is found, respondents are instead identified by row number, and lottery member IDs are matched against row position;
two or more further columns, each treated as a single categorical trait (e.g. age bracket, tenure, gender, region). Values in these columns are coerced to character and sorted alphabetically to form each trait’s factor levels, since the app has no way to infer a meaningful domain-specific order (e.g. “18-34” before “35-44”) for an arbitrary uploaded variable – a limitation with consequences for ordinal variables discussed further in Section 5.3.

For example, this thesis’s own sim_data2_cov_eq.csv begins:
"pool_member_identifier","age","tenure"
33,"18-34","Rent"
67,"18-34","Rent"
The lottery file (Panelot’s lottery.csv, or equivalent) should hold one row per possible panel, with:

a “return probability of panel” column (if applicable), giving the probability panel j would be returned were the lottery run – optional for the mosaic plots and association tests, but required for the weighted-random panel button;
one “panel member 1”, “panel member 2”, … column per selected panel member, each holding that member’s ID, matched against the sample file’s ID column (or row number, if no ID column was detected).

Correspondingly, lottery_cov_eq.csv begins:
return probability of panel,panel member 1,panel member 2,panel member 3,...
0.000890,4957,4961,4964,4966,5017,...
0.001015,6132,6166,6181,6239,6284,...
Every trait column in the sample file, not just the two currently selected for the mosaic plot, appears in the marginal bar chart described below (Figure 5.3) – so a practitioner can switch which two variables the mosaic plots compare without re-uploading anything.


Comparing intersections and marginal proportions
Once the files are uploaded, the practitioner selects any two category variables of interest (e.g. age and tenure) and the app renders a pair of mosaic plots side by side: one for the currently selected panel, one for the sample it was drawn from. These mosaic plots visualise the two-way intersection and association between the chosen variables, so that a practitioner can see at a glance whether the panel’s joint distribution of traits resembles the sample’s “shape”, or whether it is skewed in a way that marginal quota counts alone would not reveal. Figure 5.2 shows this comparison for the same most-likely panel examined manually in Figure 4.6 – the app reproduces that same blocky, uneven age-tenure structure directly, alongside the panel’s association test p-value, without requiring any code. Beneath the mosaic plots, a second window displays bar charts of every trait’s marginal proportion in the panel against the sample, across every category in the dataset, covering representativeness at the single-variable level as well.






Figure 5.2: The “Survey Sample vs. Panel” mosaic comparison, showing the most likely panel under lottery_cov_eq.csv against its survey sample – the same panel and sample compared manually in Figure 4.6.



Figure 5.3 shows the accompanying “Marginal trait distributions” view for the same panel and sample: every age bracket and tenure category side by side, with counts labelled directly on each bar. Where the mosaic plots above expose the panel’s distorted joint structure, this view confirms the panel’s single-variable marginals stay close to the sample’s throughout – precisely the gap between marginal and intersectional representativeness this thesis is concerned with (Section 4.1).






Figure 5.3: The “Marginal trait distributions” view, showing every age and tenure category’s proportion in the survey sample against the same most-likely panel under lottery_cov_eq.csv used in Figure 5.2.





Testing and browsing panels
Beyond visual inspection, the app formally tests association preservation for each panel using the tests described in Section 3.2.5, summarising each as a p-value and significance interpretation (“level of difference” from the sample), alongside the panel’s size and its probability of selection by the lottery. Panels can be browsed in several ways: sliding across all discovered panels ordered from most to least similar in association to the sample, jumping to a uniformly random panel (for arbitrary evaluation of the algorithm’s performance), jumping to a probability-weighted random panel (sidestepping the need for a separate external random number generator once a panel is to be finalised), or entering a specific panel ID directly. A further view lets the practitioner check, at an adjustable representation threshold, which intersections are missing or under-represented in the panel relative to the sample. Once a panel is chosen, its member IDs can be inspected and copied to the clipboard to continue the existing workflow (e.g. contacting selected members). Figure 5.4 shows the full set of sidebar controls behind this workflow, from file upload and variable selection down to panel navigation, member ID lookup, and the under-representation threshold slider.





 








(a) File upload, axis/fill variable selection, panel-rank slider and direct panel-ID entry.





 








(b) Random and weighted-random jump buttons, panel member ID lookup, and the adjustable under-representation threshold.





 




Figure 5.4: The sidebar’s full set of controls, split top-to-bottom into two columns for readability.





Replacing the Panelot.org selection step
In current practice, after a lottery file is generated, a practitioner takes it to a second, separate interactive page – on Panelot.org – purely to generate a random number and select one specific panel from those enumerated, then manually looks up the member IDs from the output. That step reveals nothing about which panel is being selected or how representative it is beyond the quota constraints already satisfied; it is, in effect, a black box that turns a lottery file into a single panel. Intersection Inspector is designed as a drop-in replacement: it accepts the same sample and lottery files, supports the same random (and probability-weighted random) selection as a final action, and returns the same member list a practitioner needs – while additionally providing the mosaic plots, marginal bar charts, association p-values, and under-representation checks along the way.


Benefits for new practitioners
This is particularly intended to benefit practitioners who are new to sortition or without a statistics background. Rather than trusting that satisfied quota constraints automatically mean a representative panel, the practitioner is given an interpretable visual and numerical basis for that trust – or for flagging concern – before a panel is convened. Because panels can be scrolled through and compared on their association preservation, the app can also be used diagnostically: if every available panel shows a similarly poor association to the sample, that points to the quota constraints themselves needing revision, rather than to any single unlucky draw, and may prompt the practitioner to consider whether additional surveying is needed for a more representative sample. Where a blindspot is genuinely infeasible for sortition to resolve on its own – an intersection too thin in the respondent pool for any quota-constrained panel to capture, say – the tool at least makes that limit visible, so the practitioner can weigh up whether a separate process (targeted outreach, or a specialist contribution alongside the panel) is needed to fill the gap. In this way, the app turns a previously invisible step of the sortition pipeline into a transparent, inspectable one, directly in the hands of the people already running it.

title: 5  Introducing Intersection Inspector
text:
5.3 Current limitations
The mosaic plots and association tests operate on exactly two category variables at a time, chosen from the sidebar’s axis and fill dropdowns (Figure 5.4); a dataset with more trait columns – age, tenure, gender, and region, say – cannot have its full joint structure inspected in a single view, so a practitioner steps through pairs of interest instead. This is a genuine constraint relative to the full joint distribution a panel’s representativeness ultimately depends on, not a design oversight: a fully faceted view spanning four or more variables would trade interpretability for density, and a practitioner without a statistics background is least likely to benefit from that trade. Restricting the view to two variables at a time instead gives deliberate, granular control over the “traits that matter” for a given engagement, rather than every combinatorial intersection a dataset happens to contain, most of which may be irrelevant to the community context at hand – at the cost of checking each pair in turn rather than seeing the full picture at once, a trade-off future versions could revisit by letting a practitioner flag priority combinations to surface automatically.
A further limitation stems from how uploaded trait columns are turned into factor levels: as noted above (Section 5.2.2), values are coerced to character and sorted alphabetically, since the app has no way to infer a meaningful domain-specific order for an arbitrary uploaded variable. This is immaterial for a nominal variable (gender, region, tenure), but for an ordinal variable it can produce a level order that does not match the variable’s natural progression – an income bracket column with levels “Under $20k”, “$20k-$50k”, “$50k-$100k”, “Over $100k” would not sort correctly alphabetically, nor would an agreement-scale variable running “Strongly disagree” through “Strongly agree”.
This does not affect the app’s core purpose: the mosaic plots and association tests operate correctly regardless of level order, since both the panel’s and sample’s blocks are drawn from the same (mis)ordering and remain directly comparable. What it does affect is a mosaic plot’s readability by eye – an ordinal variable with shuffled levels can look “patchier” or less monotonic than the underlying relationship warrants, since blocks that would otherwise sit adjacent and show a smooth gradient are instead scattered across the axis. A practitioner inspecting such a plot should check whether either selected variable is ordinal and read it with that re-ordering in mind, rather than inferring a lack of structure from a sorting artefact. Addressing this within the app – letting a practitioner manually specify a level order at upload time – would require per-column metadata the app’s intentionally format-agnostic file structure does not currently collect, and so is left for future refinement.
Taken together, these limitations do not undercut the app’s core contribution: Intersection Inspector still closes the central gap this thesis has identified, putting a panel’s joint structure in front of a practitioner for the first time rather than leaving it unexamined behind satisfied marginal quotas.

title: 6  Conclusion
text:
6.1 Framework and recommendations
This thesis set out from a deceptively simple question: when a sortition algorithm satisfies every quota it is given, does the panel it returns actually represent the population it was drawn from? The literature reviewed in Chapter 2 showed that decades of algorithmic development – from LEGACY through MaxiMin and MiniMax to LexiMin and Goldilocks – have answered an adjacent but different question extensively: how to make individual selection probabilities as fair and as robust to manipulation as possible. What none of these methods do is stratify, constrain, or even check their output against the combinations of traits that make up a population’s intersectional structure. The implicit assumption running through the field has been that marginal fairness, achieved at the level of each demographic category independently, is sufficient to carry intersectional representativeness along with it for free.
Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 tested that assumption directly, and found it does not hold. Across every simulated condition – independent or associated populations, equal-chance or age-skewed response – effectively every feasible panel Panelot’s LexiMin implementation could return showed an age-tenure relationship significantly different from its own survey sample, at a rate roughly an order of magnitude above what simple random sampling of the same size produces. Strikingly, this held even in the independent population, where there was no true association for a panel to represent in the first place: the distortion is a property of the quota mechanism itself, not of any one population structure or non-response pattern. Panels built to satisfy marginal quotas on age and on tenure separately were, time and again, blocky and uneven in their joint composition – a pattern invisible to the pie charts and bar charts that typically accompany reported panel composition in practice (Section 4.1), and invisible, more fundamentally, to any quota system that only ever looks at one trait at a time.
Chapter 5 responded to that finding with Intersection Inspector: a tool aimed at closing the gap between what current selection algorithms guarantee and what practitioners actually need to know before convening a panel. By placing mosaic plot comparisons, marginal bar charts, and formal association tests directly in a practitioner’s hands – alongside panel browsing, random and weighted-random selection, and an under-representation threshold – the app turns the previously invisible final step of the sortition pipeline into something inspectable, without requiring a statistics background to use.
Taken together, these chapters suggest a straightforward recommendation for practitioners and tool-builders alike: marginal quota satisfaction should be treated as necessary, but never sufficient, evidence of a representative panel. A panel that hits every category count it was asked to hit can still systematically misrepresent how those categories combine in the community it is meant to reflect, and nothing in the quota-setting or selection process as currently practised will achieve that on its own.
In practical terms, this points toward a layered framework for panel evaluation. First, quota-based selection (LexiMin, or in future, Goldilocks) remains the right tool for ensuring fair and robust selection probabilities at the marginal level – this thesis does not dispute the value of that work, only its sufficiency. Second, an intersectional check, of the kind Intersection Inspector performs, should sit between panel generation and panel convening, so that a practitioner can see whether a panel’s joint trait structure plausibly reflects its sample before members are contacted, rather than discovering a skew only once deliberation is already underway. Third, where a specific intersectional combination is known to matter for an engagement’s context – a particular minority subgroup, say – this thesis’s results suggest that relying on marginal quotas to deliver it incidentally is optimistic at best; deliberate joint-quota constraints, or supplementary recruitment targeted at that intersection, are more defensible routes than trusting the selection mechanism to produce it as a byproduct.

title: 6  Conclusion
text:
6.2 Limitations
Several limitations bound how far these findings should be read. The simulation used two categorical variables – age and tenure – chosen for their resemblance to variables genuinely used in sortition practice, but real panels are typically built against three, five, or more demographic categories simultaneously; the discrepancy documented here is expected to compound, not relax, as the intersectional space grows while panel size stays fixed. However, that expectation was not itself tested at higher dimensionality (Chapter 3). Likewise, response rates were deliberately elevated well above what civic lotteries typically see in the field, to keep respondent cells populated enough to isolate the algorithm’s own behaviour; this makes the reported distortion a conservative, best-case estimate rather than an upper bound, and the association strengths introduced into the simulated populations were fixed at values chosen for visibility rather than drawn from, or validated against, any specific real-world dataset (Chapter 3).
Intersection Inspector itself carries its own, openly acknowledged constraints (Section 5.3). It inspects two variables’ joint structure at a time, rather than the full multivariate intersection a panel’s representativeness ultimately rests on. It also sorts uploaded trait levels alphabetically, which can misorder ordinal variables and make an association harder to read by eye – though the underlying statistical tests remain valid regardless of level order. Both are deliberate trade-offs in favour of interpretability for non-specialist users, but they mean the app diagnoses the problem this thesis identifies more thoroughly than it solves it outright.

title: 6  Conclusion
text:
6.3 Future research
A natural next step is extending the simulation framework beyond two variables, to establish whether, and how severely, the intersectional distortion observed here scales with additional demographic categories – and whether it does so uniformly or concentrates in particular combinations with many trait levels. The Goldilocks algorithm, not yet publicly available at the time of writing, is also worth revisiting once released: it addresses a different problem (robustness to manipulation) to the one this thesis raises, but it remains an open question whether its joint handling of selection-probability ceilings and floors incidentally improves, worsens, or leaves unchanged the intersectional preservation documented here. More broadly, this thesis’s central finding motivates a more direct line of work: selection methods that explicitly incorporate joint, intersectional constraints alongside marginal quotas, rather than treating intersectionality purely as something to check for after the fact. One emerging example is Diversimax (Matar 2025), which uses mixed integer programming to select panels that explicitly minimise imbalance across every intersectional combination of demographic traits, rather than optimising selection probabilities at the marginal level alone; it is not evaluated in detail here, since it has yet to see the kind of practitioner adoption LexiMin has. However, it is also worth treating cautiously rather than as a straightforward replacement: optimising for intersectional balance alone, without also bounding how unequal individual selection probabilities can become, risks reopening the same extreme-probability and manipulation vulnerabilities that motivated MaxiMin, MiniMax, LexiMin and Goldilocks in the first place – a panel could end up intersectionally balanced only because some individuals were given a far higher selection chance than others to fill sparse cells. Reconciling intersectional balance with that fairness guarantee looks like the more productive target than optimising for either alone.
On the tooling side, a practical next step is packaging this thesis’s LexiMin implementation as a proper R package and integrating panel selection directly into Intersection Inspector, rather than requiring a practitioner to generate a lottery file via the separate Panelot.org interface before uploading it to the app. Collapsing today’s two-tool workflow into a single environment – covering both panel generation and intersectional evaluation – would remove a point of friction for practitioners, and would make it straightforward to extend the same integration to Goldilocks or Diversimax as those become more broadly available.

title: 6  Conclusion
text:
6.4 Closing remarks
It is worth being plain about what this thesis is, and is not, arguing. The fairness and robustness advances surveyed in Chapter 2 are genuine achievements, and nothing here suggests abandoning them. LexiMin’s maximisation of selection probabilities, and Goldilocks’ guard against manipulation, solve real problems that mattered enough to motivate a decade of algorithmic development. But a selection mechanism being fair is a different property from the panel it produces being representative, and this thesis has tried to show, explicitly, that the gap between the two is not merely theoretical. Optimising who gets a chance to be selected is not the same question as asking who, collectively, ends up involved – and whether the particular mix of people assembled actually reflects the community whose voice the process claims to amplify.
Representation, in other words, is not just a matter of getting the proportions right on each axis taken separately; it is a matter of getting the people right, in all the ways their identities and circumstances combine. A panel can be perfectly fair by the numbers and still quietly leave an entire slice of a community’s lived experience unheard, simply because no one checked whether the categories were ever meant to be looked at together. If sortition’s promise is a seat for everyone, a fair lottery is not the end of the question – it is only the beginning. The real test is who actually ends up on the panel, with their thoughts and feelings heard. So before the next panel is called fair and finished, it is worth pausing to ask: am I in the room?

title: Appendix A — Iterative proportional fitting (raking) derivation
text:
This appendix gives the full iterative update rule underlying the raking step summarised in Chapter 3, used to restore the age and tenure marginal targets \mathbf p_A and \mathbf p_T after the associated population’s exponential seeding adjustment (Equation 3.4) disturbs them.
Initialising P^{(0)}_{\text{rake}} = \tilde P, each raking iteration r = 0, 1, 2, \dots performs two rescaling passes,

P^{(r + 1/2)}(a, t) \;=\; P^{(r)}_{\text{rake}}(a, t) \cdot \frac{p_{A_a}}{\sum_{t'} P^{(r)}_{\text{rake}}(a, t')}, \qquad
P^{(r+1)}_{\text{rake}}(a, t) \;=\; P^{(r+1/2)}(a, t) \cdot \frac{p_{T_t}}{\sum_{a'} P^{(r+1/2)}(a', t)},
\tag{A.1}
